editorial.headline: Ornamental Plant Farming With a Clear National Opening
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the cultivation of living ornamental foliage, flowers, and transplantable turf, with national PMA access and no Bali moratorium block in the record.
editorial.body:
This activity is the agricultural side of the ornamental plant economy: the cultivation of living foliage plants, flowering ornamentals, and plants grown for decorative use. The record gives a broad, concrete field of activity, from bonsai, monstera, philodendron, dracaena, cordyline, anthurium foliage, ferns, aglaonema, sansevieria, caladium, and palms to flowering plants such as orchids, roses, adenium, flowering anthurium, euphorbia, and ixora. It also covers planting for ornamental purposes and grassed land prepared for transplanting. In plain terms, this is not a retail shop category and not a landscape-design description; it is farming or cultivation where the product is ornamental life.

The operating scope is also written as an integrated agricultural sequence. It includes land preparation, planting, maintenance, harvesting, and post-harvest activity when those steps are carried out as one chain of activity. That matters because the activity is defined by the cultivation process, not merely by the beauty or market value of the plants. A founder using this classification should be able to recognise a farm, nursery, or grower operation inside the wording: the work begins with soil or growing media and continues through care, harvest, and post-harvest handling.

On scale, the record is unusually straightforward. The activity is open across Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar scales. That means the category is not framed only for large plantations or only for small growers; the same activity language can describe a modest ornamental nursery as well as a larger cultivation operation, provided the real business activity remains within the farming and cultivation scope described above. The national investment position is also direct: the PMA status is TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. There is no capped foreign stake in the record, so the national reading is a clean foreign-open position rather than a conditional minority opening.

The Bali picture is more specific, and here the honest answer is favourable. The province-wide moratorium described in the record blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, but this activity is marked as not blocked: its Bali status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the stated reason is that OSS risk at Besar scale is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not blocked by the moratorium. For a foreign founder, the practical editorial point is simple: this ornamental plant farming activity is nationally open to PMA up to 100%, and the Bali moratorium field in the record does not close it. The remaining judgment is therefore not a hidden ownership warning; it is whether the planned operation truly fits the cultivation chain described in the scope.
